To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Fnr is a [4Fe4S] cluster-containing transcriptional activator that forms ternary complex with PlcR and ResD.
Fnr binds a Fe-S cluster and forms a complex with ResD or PlcR.

the [4Fe–4S]2+-containing Fnr binds to the promoter regions of enterotoxin-encoding genes, interacts with ResD and forms a ternar complex with PlcR, and that these properties are not affected by the presence or absence of the [4Fes-4S] 2+ cluster.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the redox regulation in the pathogenesis of B. cereus.
the redox regulation in Bacillus cereus and the molecular mechanism of the regulation.
the regulation of virulence factors in Bacillus cereus and the molecular mechanisms of action of the redox regulators ResD and Fnr.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Fnr is not a classical transcriptional regulator, and that the Fe-S cluster does not have an obvious role in the regulation of enterotoxins in B. cereus.
the Fe-S cluster of Fnr is not required for binding to DNA, but may be required for interaction with ResD and/or PlcR.
B. cereus is a model organism that can be used to study the redox regulation and the role of Fe-S proteins in the regulation of virulence genes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the [4Fe4S]2+-cluster of B. cereus is not essential for the transcriptional regulation of the enterotoxin genes.
the [4Fe4S]2+-cluster is not required for Fnr-dependent regulation in B. cereus.
the Fe-S cluster is required to stabilize the DNA binding activity of Fnr.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Fnr-dependent expression of hbl and/or nhe is likely to be controlled by a mechanism other than DNA binding of the [4fe-4S] protein to the promoter regions of these genes.
Fnr is a novel member of the Crf/Fnr family of proteins that does not bind a [2Fe-2S] cluster but a [4Fe4S] cluster.
B. cereus is the first bacterium for which the Fnr-dependent activation of a gene cluster is shown to be independent of the incorporation of a Fe-S cluster.
